paper_title: Learning and Reasoning with Geometry: How Generation Helps Spatial Understanding

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Image and video generators can produce spatially consistent visual content, but how to use this capability to improve spatial understanding remains underexplored. We study this problem from two perspectives: geometric supervision during training and explicit geometric evidence during inference. To this end, we introduce a unified geometric understanding and generation model (GeoUG) that integrates depth and multi-view generation with spatial understanding. First, we design a multi-scale depth codec that enables metric-depth generation using a pretrained visual autoencoder, and show that joint training yields task-dependent gains in spatial understanding. Second, we introduce 3DCueBench to control geometric difficulty while balancing selected 2D cues, and find that generated depth provides larger reasoning gains on questions requiring fine-grained geometric discrimination. Building on this finding, we develop adaptive interleaved reasoning, in which GeoUG first drafts an answer and then decides whether to generate geometric evidence to confirm or revise it. We train this decision through reinforcement learning, balancing accuracy gains over retaining the draft against generation cost. GeoUG achieves circular accuracies of 97.9%, 90.8%, and 94.2% on CV-Bench-3D, 3DCueBench, and DA-2K with fewer generation calls than always generating.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Foundation models increasingly learn from multimodal observations of the world, extending beyond the knowledge conveyed through language [2, 3, 64]. While language efficiently expresses concepts and relations, it often leaves the fine-grained geometry of physical scenes and their continuous changes underspecified [60]. Learning to predict visual observations offers complementary source of supervision, requiring models to capture spatial structure and how it changes across views and over time. Recent advances in visual generation and editing [26, 50, 61] suggest growing capabilities to maintain coherent scene structure through such changes. Recent studies of multimodal pretraining further highlight the potential for generation and understanding to benefit from shared learning, while revealing that knowledge transfer is asymmetric and task-dependent [28, 64]. This raises concrete question for geometry, which underlies both coherent visual generation and accurate spatial judgments: how can geometric generation help models learn spatial relations and reason about them? To address this question, we examine geometric generation during both learning and reasoning. During learning, visual question answering (VQA) typically supervises the specific relations queried in scene, whereas 1 Figure 1 Learning and reasoning with geometry. Learning with geometry (left): GeoUG co-trains spatial understanding with geometric generation of new views and metric depth, improving MindCube and DA-2K (Section 5.1). Reasoning with geometry (middle and right): GeoUG first drafts an answer, then decides whether to generate depth. Here it generates depth, queries 3D distances from the generated depth lifted to 3D, and revises the incorrect draft. Far right: comparison of GeoUG with Marigold [36], DA3 [43], and Seed-2.0 [13] on DA-2K [77]. generating depth or images from other viewpoints provides supervision over richer scene structure and its visual consequences. This motivates examining how different geometric generation objectives contribute to spatial understanding. During reasoning, generated geometry can provide explicit intermediate representations from which depth and distance measurements can be obtained to support spatial judgments. We therefore ask when using this additional evidence improves an answer and whether models can learn to acquire it selectively. These two perspectives connect learning spatial relations from geometric supervision with reasoning over generated geometry. To study these two roles, we develop GeoUG (Figure 1), unified model that integrates spatial understanding with metric-depth generation and view-generation tasks. To enable metric-depth generation, we introduce Multi-scale Metric Depth Codec (MMDC). MMDC encodes metric depth into bounded three-channel representation compatible with pretrained visual autoencoder, with each channel operating at different depth scale. During training, we jointly optimize next-token prediction objective for spatial understanding and flow-matching objective for geometric generation. Comparing different geometric generation objectives reveals task-dependent benefits: metric-depth generation primarily improves depth-related spatial abilities, whereas view generation benefits spatial understanding across viewpoints. During inference, GeoUG uses generated metric depth as explicit geometric evidence. To characterize when this evidence is useful, we introduce 3DCueBench, which balances cases in which selected 2D cues agree or conflict with the true 3D relations across different geometric difficulty levels. We find that generated depth provides larger gains when the compared objects have smaller depth or distance gaps. Motivated by this finding, we develop adaptive interleaved reasoning, in which GeoUG first drafts an answer and then decides whether to generate geometric evidence to confirm or revise it. We train this draft-conditioned policy using reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) [20], introducing decision-specific advantage that compares generation with retaining the draft while accounting for generation cost. By acquiring geometric evidence selectively, GeoUG retains most of the gains from always generating while requiring fewer generation calls. It achieves circular accuracies of 97.9%, 90.8%, and 94.2% on CV-Bench-3D [62], 3DCueBench, and DA-2K [77], respectively. Together, these findings highlight the task-dependent benefits of geometric supervision during training and the value of selectively acquiring geometric evidence during inference. Our main contributions are as follows: We study geometric generation as both training supervision and reasoning evidence, analyzing the taskdependent benefits of different generation objectives and how inference gains vary with geometric difficulty. We introduce GeoUG, which integrates metric-depth and camera-conditioned multi-view generation into unified understanding and generation model. Using the draft answer as reference, reinforcement learning balances accuracy gains against generation costs to support on-demand generation and use of geometric 2 evidence. We introduce 3DCueBench, which controls geometric difficulty while balancing the validity of selected 2D cues, enabling more targeted evaluation of spatial reasoning. Across three spatial understanding benchmarks, GeoUG achieves the highest circular accuracy among the evaluated vision-language models, while using fewer generation calls and maintaining accuracy close to or above the always-generate configuration.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Unified Understanding and Generation. Unified multimodal models combine language prediction with visual generation [76, 90]. BAGEL uses Mixture-of-Transformer-Experts (MoT) architecture with specialized understanding and generation experts [21]. MetaMorph reports mutual benefits with asymmetric contributions from understanding and generation data [63]. Recent pretraining studies investigate cross-modal complementarity, knowledge transfer, and conditions for synergy [28, 64]. We examine these interactions specifically through geometric generation and spatial understanding. Generation for Understanding and Reasoning. Generative supervision improves visual understanding through reconstruction [67] and semantic proxy tasks [82]. At inference time, MVoT generates visual reasoning traces [41], while visual world-modeling studies identify task-dependent benefits of generated intermediates [73]. COOPER learns relative-depth and segmentation generation alongside adaptive interleaved spatial reasoning [86]. For cross-view reasoning, recent work examines synthesized viewpoints and whether models effectively use generated visual evidence [78, 85]. Our work develops multi-scale metric-depth encoding and studies depth and view generation as training supervision and generated depth as evidence during inference, emphasizing how geometric difficulty and generation errors affect downstream benefits. This analysis distinguishes the benefits of learning geometric representations from those of explicitly generating and interpreting them at test time. Spatial Understanding and Reasoning. Existing approaches strengthen spatial capabilities through geometric representations and spatial supervision. VLM-3R incorporates geometry encoder to extract implicit 3D tokens from monocular video [22]. From data perspective, SpatialVLM, Visual Spatial Tuning, and OpenSpatial construct spatial instruction data to improve perception and reasoning [18, 47, 79]. Their instruction targets provide spatially sparse supervision through selected attributes, objects, and relations, rather than dense per-pixel geometric targets. We complement such supervision with metric-depth and multi-view generation objectives, providing dense visual supervision for learning geometry and enabling generated representations to support spatial reasoning.

sections.title: 3 Method
sections.content: We investigate how geometric generation helps spatial understanding through learning and reasoning with geometry. We build GeoUG on BAGEL [21], unified understanding and generation model. For learning with geometry, we study co-training configurations that jointly optimize spatial understanding and geometric generation task, using cross-entropy loss on text tokens and flow-matching loss for visual generation. For reasoning with geometry, the model first drafts an answer and then decides whether to generate depth and query geometric measurements to confirm or revise it. We train this decision to balance answer correctness against generation cost.

sections.title: 3.1 Geometric Generation Tasks
sections.content: We unify geometric generation tasks through common visual output representation and velocity-prediction objective based on flow matching [46, 48]. Each target is represented as three-channel image: an encoded metric-depth map or an RGB target view. Following BAGEL, frozen VAE encodes this target into latents, and the model predicts the flow velocity from noise-corrupted latents conditioned on the input image, task instruction, and timestep. At inference, the predicted velocity field transforms noise into target latents, which the VAE decodes into the visual output. The tasks thus share one generation mechanism and differ only in conditioning and target. 3 Figure 2 Multi-scale depth encoding. (a) single pivot compresses depth differences far from its scale. (b) second channel with larger pivot separates depths saturated in the first. We study two forms of geometric supervision within this framework. Metric-depth generation captures the depths of visible surfaces, providing explicit geometry for spatial measurement. View generation captures changes in spatial layout, visibility, and occlusion induced by change of viewpoint. In camera-conditioned multi-view generation (multi-view for short), the target viewpoint is given by camera-motion instruction, which we derive from relative camera poses to account for both rotation and translation (Appendix D.2). In exo-to-ego generation, the target viewpoint is that of person in third-person image; generating that persons first-person view requires perspective taking, imagining the scene from another observers viewpoint (Appendix D.3). Multi-scale Metric Depth Codec. To represent metric depth within this common image interface, we introduce the Multi-scale Metric Depth Codec (MMDC). It maps depth into bounded three-channel representation compatible with the pretrained VAE and converts the generated output back into metric depth, preserving consistent physical scale across images. Generative depth estimators such as Marigold [36] normalize each ground-truth depth map using its scenespecific 2nd and 98th percentiles. Given metric ground-truth depth value at pixel, they construct the normalized target = 2 ((d d2)/(d98 d2) 1/2), where d2 and d98 are computed independently for each depth map. This produces an affine-invariant target compatible with the bounded input range of an RGB VAE. Because the metric values of d2 and d98 are unavailable at inference, the predicted normalized depth cannot be converted back to metric depth without recovering the unknown scene-specific scale and shift. We instead encode the same metric depth > 0 as normalized value (1, 1) using fixed, invertible transformation with fixed pivot > 0, where and are both in metres: = + (1, 1), = 1 + 1 . (1) Every encoded value now has consistent metric meaning across images, allowing the generated representation to be decoded into metric depth map at inference. However, single pivot compresses relative depth differences away from its characteristic scale, amplifying reconstruction errors during decoding, as shown in Figure 2(a). MMDC addresses this by exploiting the three input channels of the RGB VAE. Rather than repeat single-scale encoding three times, we assign each channel different depth scale: Yi = ci + ci , (c1, c2, c3) = (2, 8, 32) m. (2) The channels provide complementary precision across depth ranges: where one channel approaches saturation, another can better distinguish depth differences (Figure 2). The pivots are fixed across datasets, and the resulting representation fits the pretrained VAE without architecture changes. For decoding, we invert each generated channel and fuse the per-channel estimates: ˆdi = ci 1 + ˆYi 1 ˆYi , wi = (1 ˆY 2 )2, ˆd = (cid:80) (cid:80) ˆdi wi wi . (3) The weight is largest near channels pivot and decreases towards saturation, allowing different channels to contribute at different depth scales. More details are provided in Appendix B. MMDC introduces no learned parameters. During training, encoded depth maps serve as targets through the frozen VAE encoder. At inference, MMDC converts the VAE-decoded outputs into metric depth maps for geometric measurement and interleaved reasoning. 4 Figure 3 When does generation help? sections.title: 3.2 Interleaved Geometric Reasoning
sections.content: We next turn from geometric supervision during training to using generated depth as evidence for spatial reasoning at inference time. Before designing the reasoning procedure, we address two questions through two pilot studies: Pilot I: When Does Generation Help? We compare direct answering (Direct) with reasoning that always generates depth before answering (Always-generate) on CV-Bench-3D [62] and 3DCueBench (Section 4.1). We measure difficulty by the relative gap = da db max(da, db) , (4) where da and db are the camera depths or distances to the anchor being compared. We group questions in both datasets into bins according to their relative gap. Figure 3 shows larger gains from generation-assisted reasoning over direct answering on difficult questions with smaller gaps. On easier questions, direct answering already achieves high accuracy, while generation-assisted reasoning provides limited gains and sometimes reduces accuracy. This degradation may result from errors in generated depth or geometric measurements. These findings motivate adaptive interleaved reasoning, in which the model decides when to generate geometric evidence. Pilot II: Can the Model Tell When It Needs Geometry? The ground-truth gap is unavailable at test time, so the model must decide whether to generate from its own reasoning context. straightforward approach is before-answer policy, which chooses between direct answering and generation-assisted reasoning before producing an answer (Figure 4a, top). To evaluate whether the policy identifies questions that benefit from generation, we use its generation probability: the probability of choosing the depth-generation branch at the <DECIDE> step in Figure 4a. For each generation budget, questions with the highest generation probabilities receive generation-assisted reasoning, while the remainder are answered directly, yielding the orange Before curve in Figure 4b. In contrast, the green Gap curve ranks questions by their ground-truth relative gaps in ascending order, prioritizing the smallest-gap questions. The vertical axis reports the fraction of the accuracy gain from always generating retained by each selection strategy on 3DCueBench (the detailed protocol can be found in Appendix C). The Gap reference requires ground-truth geometry and is unavailable at test time. Random selection retains fraction of the gain equal to the generation budget in expectation. 5 At 50% generation budget, the before-answer policy retains only 55% of the gain from always generating, close to the 50% expected from random selection (Figure 4b). Reinforcement learning also fails to produce selective generation in our runs: the policy tends to generate for either almost no questions or almost all questions (Figure 4c). These results suggest that, in this setup, the before-answer policy does not learn to identify questions that benefit from generation. We draw inspiration from reflective reasoning in chain-ofthought, where model forms tentative answer and subsequently reconsiders it before reaching final answer. This motivates us to use the tentative answer as draft and place the generation decision at this point of reconsideration. Specifically, we introduce draft-conditioned policy, which first produces an initial draft from the input image and question without depth generation, then decides whether to retain it as the final answer or generate geometric evidence to verify or revise it (Figure 4a, bottom). Under the same ranking protocol and 50% generation budget, this policy retains 86% of the gain from always generating, compared with 55% for the before-answer policy (Figure 4b). Each policys retained gain is normalized by its own direct and always-generate accuracies. We instantiate this policy with depth generation. For example, to decide which of two objects is closer, the model generates depth map, decodes it into metric depth using MMDC, and queries the objects depths before confirming or revising its draft. Learning When to Generate. We train the draft-conditioned policy in two stages. First, we cold-start the policy through supervised fine-tuning on chain-of-thought (CoT) sequences that follow the draft-conditioned reasoning format: an initial answer draft, decision on whether to generate depth, and final answer that either retains the draft or uses generated geometric evidence to verify or revise it. Draft tokens are excluded from the training loss (Appendix C). Starting from this initialization, we use GSPO-based reinforcement learning [87] to optimize the policys generation decisions for the accuracycost trade-off. The reward is ri = ci λai, where ci {0, 1} indicates final-answer correctness, ai {0, 1} indicates generation, and λ is the generation cost. sections.title: 4 Evaluation
sections.content: 4.1 3DCueBench: Controlled Evaluation of Geometric Reasoning VLMs may rely on 2D image-plane relationships to answer 3D spatial questions without understanding the underlying 3D structure. Figure 5(a,b) shows two such shortcuts, lower in the image is closer and closer in the image plane is closer in 3D, each contradicted by the scenes 3D geometry. In our analysis of CV-Bench-3D, choosing the object with the lower bounding-box bottom correctly answers 85.3% of Depth questions (Figure 5(c)), and no question has relative gap below 0.16. Current VLMs follow such cues: on 3DCueBench Distance questions where the rule gives the wrong answer, Seed-2.0-Lite [13] and GPT-5.5 [51] reach only 37.0% and 35.7% (Figure 5(d)). This makes it difficult to determine whether high accuracy reflects geometric reasoning or reliance on image-plane cues. We therefore introduce 3DCueBench, benchmark of 800 carefully selected questions in two tasks: Depth compares the camera depths of two targets, and Distance compares their 3D distances to an anchor. In half of the questions (cue-consistent), the 2D rules used to construct the benchmark favor the correct answer; in the other half (cue-conflicting), they favor the wrong answer. Each rule therefore achieves 50% accuracy, so models must go beyond these rules to perform well. To control difficulty, we sample questions across intervals of the relative gap (Equation 4), keeping cue-consistent and cue-conflicting questions balanced within each interval (Appendix E.2).

Co-training also teaches geometrically controlled generation. Figure 7 shows the three geometric generation abilities. For depth generation, the generated metric depth preserves the scene layout, such as the receding arches and free-standing pillars of the hallway and the overhanging roof of the terrace, and back-projects to coherent 3D reconstructions. For multi-view generation, the original BAGEL [21] often returns view close to the input, whereas our model moves the camera as instructed and brings new content into view: it swings the view around the cannon when moving right and turning left, and pulls back to reveal the shoreline when moving backward, while BAGEL nearly copies the input. For exo-to-ego generation, BAGEL depicts the described person, whereas our model renders the court from that persons viewpoint, looking up at the hoop during layup or down at the ball and the goal before penalty kick. Quantitatively, our models improve PSNR by up to 1.25 dB on multi-view generation and from 7.75 to 12.41 dB on exo-to-ego generation (Appendix E.1); depth accuracy is evaluated in Section 5.4, and more examples are in Appendix A.

sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: We studied how geometric generation supports spatial understanding through both learning and reasoning, using GeoUG as unified framework. During training, joint learning with depth and multi-view generation yields task-dependent gains. During inference, our evaluation on 3DCueBench shows larger benefits from generated depth on questions requiring fine-grained geometric discrimination. Building on these findings, we developed adaptive interleaved reasoning, where draft-conditioned policy learns through reinforcement learning to balance accuracy gains against generation cost. Across three benchmarks, this policy maintains accuracy close to or above always generating with fewer generation calls. These results highlight two complementary roles for geometric generation: supervision for learning spatial relations and evidence acquired selectively during reasoning.

sections.title: A Qualitative Results
sections.content: Figure 9 shows predicted depth maps and their corresponding colored 3D reconstructions. The examples preserve recognizable scene layout, including the tiered seating in the lecture hall, tables in front of the courtyard facade, and the recessed doorway in the office. Depth boundaries follow many visible object contours, while the reconstructions also expose gaps and distortions near some boundaries. These examples illustrate recovered spatial structure without serving as quantitative test of metric calibration. Real training data for the metric depth estimation are commonly derived from either LiDAR scans or Structure-from-Motion (SfM) reconstructions: LiDAR suffers from sensorcamera synchronization errors that corrupt depth along object boundaries, while SfM fails on reflective surfaces, thin structures, and sharp discontinuities, leaving holes or oversmoothed regions. depth estimator trained on synthetic data avoids both issuescolor and depth are exactly registered by construction and fine local geometry is preservedbut it predicts relative depth only up to an unknown affine transform. D.3 Exo-to-Ego Generation Data Exo-to-ego generation is form of multi-view generation that requires perspective taking: the target viewpoint is specified by another observer in the scene rather than by camera-motion instruction, and the model must imagine what that observer sees. We build exo-to-ego pairs from Ego-Exo4D [27], which records each take with static third-person (exo) cameras and head-mounted first-person (ego) camera. Each pair consists of an exo frame and the ego frame captured at the same time step. VLM describes the camera wearer in the exo frame, including appearance, action, and surroundings, and turns the description into an instruction that asks for that persons first-person view. We remove pairs whose instruction contains unparsed VLM output, leaked templates, or references to markers that are not drawn on the image. The resulting set contains 171,558 pairs covering sports, bike repair, cooking, health care, music, and dance. The ego target is resized to 512 512. Figure 22 shows examples. The task requires the model to locate the described person in the exo view, infer where that person is looking, and render the scene from the new viewpoint. The ego target therefore contains the objects in front of the person, often at large viewpoint change from the exo camera, rather than the person themselves.

Each pair consists of source view, target view, and camera-motion instruction 33 built from the relative pose of the two views with the procedure of Appendix D.2, for example Move the camera forward 1.81 and rotate the camera left 36 degrees. The model generates the target view from the source view and the instruction. Exo-to-ego generation. The benchmark contains 469 pairs from Ego-Exo4D [27]. Each pair consists of an exo frame, the synchronized ego frame, and an instruction of the form Show me the ego view of person description. The model generates the 512 512 ego view. Metrics. We compare each generated image with the ground-truth target using PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS [84] with an AlexNet backbone. Generated images are resized to the target resolution before scoring. Generation uses 50 denoising steps with the default classifier-free guidance of BAGEL [21] (text scale 4.0, image scale 2.0). Tables 7 and 8 compare the original BAGEL with our models, which are the same models shown in Figures 10 and 11. On multi-view generation, our model improves all three metrics on every source, with the largest gain on RealEstate10K (+1.25 dB PSNR, 0.071 LPIPS). On exo-to-ego generation, BAGEL scores much lower (7.75 dB PSNR), consistent with its tendency to depict the described person rather than that persons view (Figure 11). Our model raises PSNR to 12.41 dB and lowers LPIPS from 0.839 to 0.670. These pixel and perceptual metrics reward matching the exact target view, and absolute values remain low because single source image and instruction do not fully determine the target. sections.content: F.1 Generation Pretraining Followed by Understanding SFT Generation pretraining alone does not reliably provide better initialization for downstream understanding SFT. Together with the task-dependent gains from co-training, these results suggest that jointly optimizing generation and understanding may be important for transferring geometric knowledge. We compare three initializations: the original BAGEL [21] model, model pretrained for 6,000 steps on depth generation, and model pretrained for 6,000 steps on multi-view generation. All three then undergo the same understanding-only SFT, using the same data and hyperparameters, with no generation objective during this stage. At steps 1,0006,000, cumulative SFT CE tokens are 6.29M, 12.48M, 18.77M, 25.00M, 31.10M, and 37.34M for each arm. The preceding generation stage is excluded from the plotted token budget; total training compute is therefore not matched. Figure 26 Generation pretraining followed by understanding SFT. Six EMA checkpoints per run, plotted against SFT CE tokens. CV-Bench-3D, DA-2K, and MindCube use circular accuracy; MMSI camera motion uses ordinary accuracy (n = 74). At the final SFT checkpoint, both generation-initialized models are 0.34 percentage points below the original initialization on CV-Bench-3D [62]. Depth and multi-view initialization are lower by 2.61 and 3.38 points on DA-2K [77], and by 2.70 and 6.76 points on MMSI [80] camera motion, respectively. MindCube [70] shows different pattern: the generation-initialized models retain small advantages of 0.87 and 2.02 points, but accuracy declines after the first evaluated SFT checkpoint for all three arms. These results concern transfer under the chosen SFT procedure, rather than the quality of the learned representations in isolation. Since the sequential and co-training experiments are not fully matched, they do not establish that co-training is necessary. F.2 Visual and Textual Referring Formats We report all seven evaluated open-source models under both visual and textual referring formats. CV-Bench3D [62] uses overlaid boxes in its visual version and textual box coordinates in its textual version; both contain the same 1,200 questions (600 Depth and 600 Distance). DA-2K [77] uses colored point markers in the visual version and textual point coordinates in the textual version, with 2,068 questions. Textual coordinates follow each models input convention, including conversion to resized-image pixels where required. Sensitivity varies across models and tasks. Textual referring does not uniformly increase or decrease accuracy. On CV-Bench-3D, five models score lower with textual coordinates, while both SenseNova configurations score higher. Referring format therefore affects measured performance and should be held fixed when comparing systems. DA-2K also probes marker and answer consistency. Qwen2.5-VLs 9.8% visual circular accuracy is accompanied by strong preference for the green point (93.5% of responses), while its mean accuracy over visual variants is 53.3%. Its large Textual-minus-Visual difference therefore cannot be interpreted as an equally large gain in geometric understanding. F.3 External Depth Tools We also evaluate whether supplying an existing VLM with external depth measurements yields comparable performance. DA3 [43] (DA3NESTED-GIANT-LARGE-1.1) predicts depth, shared measurement procedure extracts object depths and pairwise 3D distances, and the measurements are supplied as text to the answering VLM. Table 14 reports the resulting system performance alongside the corresponding direct-answer baselines. Qwen2.5-VL uses different input resolutions with and without DA3, and BAGEL prompts also differ; these are reference system comparisons rather than controlled estimates of the tool effect. Their scores remain below GeoUG and below answering from the DA3 measurements alone (last row) on all three benchmarks. This comparison shows that the evaluated combination of external measurements and an existing VLM is insufficient to match GeoUG; it does not establish that self-generated depth is intrinsically more accurate than DA3 or isolate the effect of tool use from prompting, resolution, and training differences.
